B. Measure outcomes across relevant groups and intersectional slices, investigate proxy features and process effects, mitigate the disparity, and require fairness thresholds before release
C. Remove all demographic data from evaluation so the disparity is no longer visible
D. Release immediately and address fairness only if an individual user files a complaint
questions.explanation: This original scenario applies Microsoft's fairness principle to measured outcomes. Excluding a protected attribute does not prove fairness because correlated features and business processes can still produce group disparities. Representative, disaggregated evaluation, mitigation, documented thresholds, and ongoing monitoring provide decision evidence that aggregate accuracy cannot.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Fairness measurement and release decisions

questions.question: An employee-facing agent ranks benefit options from policy documents. The team wants transparency but proposes publishing the complete system prompt and model chain-of-thought to every user. Which design better supports transparency without creating unnecessary security and privacy risk?
options: A. Provide no notice because users can infer that the interface uses AI
B. Explain that AI is being used, its intended purpose and material limitations, the information and citations supporting the result, and how users can correct or escalate an outcome
C. Publish hidden instructions, credentials, and private reasoning traces as the only form of explanation
D. Display only the model's product name because technical identity fully explains each recommendation
questions.explanation: This original question distinguishes useful transparency from disclosure of sensitive implementation details. People should know when AI is involved, what the system is intended to do, its consequential limitations, what grounds a result, and how to seek correction or human help. Transparency does not require exposing secrets or private internal reasoning.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Actionable transparency and user recourse

questions.question: A company deploys a third-party model through an agent that recommends whether suppliers should be suspended. The sponsor says the model provider is accountable for every business outcome because it built the model. What governance design should the architect require?
options: A. Assign an internal accountable owner, document intended use and impact, define approval and escalation authority, monitor outcomes, and retain evidence of risk and release decisions
B. Transfer all accountability to the model provider and omit internal controls
C. Let the agent assign accountability dynamically after each recommendation
D. Make individual end users solely accountable even when they cannot inspect, override, or appeal the recommendation
questions.explanation: This original scenario applies accountability to the organization that designs and deploys the complete business solution. Supplier contracts and provider controls are inputs, but they don't replace named internal ownership, impact assessment, decision authority, operational monitoring, incident handling, and auditable approvals.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Organizational accountability for third-party AI

questions.question: A claims agent routes high-impact denial recommendations to a human reviewer, but the interface hides supporting evidence and uncertainty, allows ten seconds per case, and provides no reject or escalation action. The team calls this human-in-the-loop. What should change?
options: A. Remove review because a fast approval screen already proves accountability
B. Give reviewers relevant evidence, limitations, sufficient time, and authority to reject, override, or escalate; then monitor review quality and automation bias
C. Keep the interface and count every timeout as reviewer approval
D. Replace the reviewer with a second call to the same model
questions.explanation: This original human-oversight scenario tests whether intervention is meaningful rather than ceremonial. Effective review requires context, time, competence, and real authority to stop or change a consequential action. Monitoring overrides, escalations, and reviewer behavior helps detect rubber-stamping and automation bias.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Meaningful human oversight and automation bias

questions.question: A production support agent's content guardrail blocks too many benign technical answers. Operations proposes disabling the guardrail globally to restore completion rates. What is the best response?
options: A. Disable every guardrail because business metrics take priority after launch

B. Evaluate representative benign and harmful cases, identify the triggering policy and business risk, make the smallest justified configuration change, stage the rollout, and monitor safety and quality
C. Ask the model to ignore blocked responses while leaving the configuration unchanged
D. Raise every threshold to its least restrictive value without recording the decision
questions.explanation: This original scenario treats guardrail tuning as a governed risk decision. False positives should be measured against representative and harmful test cases, traced to the relevant control, and addressed with the narrowest justified change. Staging, documentation, and post-change monitoring protect both utility and safety.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Risk-based guardrail tuning

questions.question: When a high-risk request is blocked by a configured guardrail, an agent flow automatically rephrases the request repeatedly until one variant passes. What should the architect recommend?
options: A. Keep retrying because a later pass proves the original request was safe
B. Treat the policy block as a governed outcome, stop evasive retries, return an approved safe response or escalation path, and log the event for monitoring and review
C. Remove the event from telemetry so users cannot infer the guardrail policy
D. Grant the agent more tool permissions so it can complete the blocked request another way
questions.explanation: This original scenario distinguishes a safety-policy decision from a transient technical failure. Automatically mutating blocked input until it passes can circumvent the configured control. The orchestration should fail safely, provide an approved fallback or review path, and preserve telemetry for governance and tuning.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Guardrail enforcement and safe fallback

questions.question: A single Azure-hosted agent needs a credential-free identity that should be created and deleted with that compute resource. The identity will not be shared with other resources. Which identity type best matches the lifecycle requirement?
options: A. A system-assigned managed identity
B. A user-assigned managed identity shared across the subscription
C. A client secret stored in the agent instructions
D. An administrator's interactive refresh token
questions.explanation: This original selection question uses the documented managed-identity lifecycle distinction. A system-assigned identity is enabled directly on one Azure resource and is deleted with that resource. It is appropriate when the identity should not outlive or be shared by the host.
questions.topic: D3.4 / System-assigned managed identity lifecycle

questions.question: A team uses blue-green deployments for an Azure-hosted agent. Both deployment slots need the same Azure identity and downstream role assignments, and the identity must survive when either compute resource is replaced. What should the architect use?
options: A. A separate system-assigned identity for each slot and manual permission copying after every replacement
B. A user-assigned managed identity attached to both approved hosts
C. A shared storage account key embedded in both deployments
D. The release engineer's personal identity at runtime
questions.explanation: This original scenario uses the independent lifecycle and shareability of a user-assigned managed identity. The identity can be created separately, attached to multiple approved Azure resources, and retain its role assignments as hosts are replaced, without introducing application-managed credentials.
questions.topic: D3.4 / User-assigned managed identity for replaceable hosts

questions.question: An autonomous agent only reads invoice blobs from one container. Its managed identity currently has Storage Blob Data Contributor at subscription scope. Which change best follows least privilege?
options: A. Replace the assignment with the read-only data role at the narrowest scope that contains the required blobs
B. Add Owner at management-group scope so all authorization paths are covered
C. Keep write and delete permissions because managed identities are trusted by definition
D. Remove RBAC and use the subscription's billing role for blob access
questions.explanation: This original least-privilege question requires both the minimum actions and the minimum scope. A read-only workload should not receive write or delete data actions, and access to one container does not justify a subscription-wide assignment. Managed identity authenticates the workload but doesn't make excess authorization safe.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Least-privilege role and scope selection

questions.question: A read-only reporting agent and a remediation agent that can delete secrets are attached to the same user-assigned managed identity for convenience. What is the primary governance problem, and how should it be corrected?
options: A. User-assigned identities cannot be attached to multiple Azure resources, so both agents need shared API keys
B. Both agents inherit the identity's combined authorization; use separate workload identities and narrowly scoped roles when their duties and risk differ
C. Managed identities bypass Azure RBAC, so role assignments have no effect
D. The reporting agent should receive subscription Owner directly in addition to the shared identity
questions.explanation: This original cross-domain scenario exposes a reuse trap. Every host using a user-assigned identity can act with that identity's permissions. Sharing one identity across workloads with materially different duties creates privilege aggregation, weakens attribution, and lets the low-risk workload exercise high-impact authority. Separate identities preserve least privilege and clearer accountability.
questions.topic: D3.4 / Managed identity reuse and privilege aggregation

questions.question: A sales organization plans to enable an AI assistant for opportunity reviews tomorrow. Required CRM fields are incomplete, duplicate account values remain, and the SharePoint proposal library has no approved sensitivity-label scheme. The sponsor proposes enabling a small production group first and cleaning the data afterward. What should the architect recommend?
options: A. Enable the production group because limiting the audience resolves data-readiness risk
B. Complete and standardize the required source data, apply and validate the required labels and permissions, and then run a controlled pilot
C. Fine-tune a language model on the incomplete records so it can infer the missing fields
D. Replace SharePoint with a public website so sensitivity labels are unnecessary
questions.explanation: A limited audience doesn't repair unreliable or improperly governed grounding data. Data readiness is a release dependency: required fields and duplicates must be remediated, and information protection, permissions, and retrieval behavior must be validated before users rely on generated output. A controlled pilot follows those readiness checks; it doesn't replace them.
questions.topic: D1.1 / Data-readiness sequencing and sensitivity labels

questions.question: A proposed procurement agent reads public supplier catalogs and can also approve high-value purchase orders with privileged ERP access. The team wants one agent and one broad identity to simplify operations. What is the strongest reason to split the design?
options: A. Every data source requires a separate language model
B. Public retrieval and privileged approval cross materially different trust and authorization boundaries, so separate agents can enforce distinct identities, permissions, and controls
C. Multi-agent systems always cost less than single-agent systems
D. Separate agents eliminate the need for human approval of high-value purchases
questions.explanation: Agent boundaries should reflect meaningful differences in trust, authority, and risk. Separating public-information retrieval from consequential ERP approval prevents privilege aggregation and allows each workload to have its own identity, tools, guardrails, and audit path. The split is justified by the security boundary, not by an assumption that more agents are inherently better.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Multi-agent separation at trust boundaries

questions.question: A claims workflow must first extract policy facts. A coverage agent and a fraud-screening agent can then analyze those same facts independently, after which a decision agent combines both results. Which orchestration design best matches these dependencies?
options: A. Run extraction, coverage, fraud screening, and decision all in parallel
B. Run every step sequentially, including coverage and fraud screening
C. Run extraction first, fan out coverage and fraud screening in parallel, and run the decision step after both complete
D. Use a round-robin loop until any agent returns a final decision
questions.explanation: Sequential orchestration is required where one step produces input needed by another. Parallel orchestration is appropriate for independent branches that share available input. This workflow therefore uses a sequential stage, a parallel fan-out, and a synchronization point before the final dependent decision.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Sequential and parallel orchestration dependencies

questions.question: An Azure-hosted agent calls Azure Storage and Key Vault without user delegation. Operations proposes registering an application and storing its client secret in an encrypted environment variable. The host supports managed identities. Which identity design should the architect prefer?
options: A. A managed identity with only the required data-plane roles at the narrowest practical scopes
B. A service principal secret embedded in the system prompt so the agent can retrieve it
C. A shared administrator account protected by multifactor authentication
D. Storage account keys copied into the deployment pipeline
questions.explanation: Managed identities let supported Azure resources obtain Microsoft Entra tokens without the application managing credentials. This removes stored-secret rotation and exposure risk. The identity still needs explicit least-privilege authorization on Storage and Key Vault; managed identity changes authentication, not the need for scoped RBAC.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Managed identity instead of stored workload secrets

questions.question: A maker has the technical components and environment privileges needed to create a custom connector for an external payroll API. The connector is created successfully, but the solution can't use it with a Dataverse connector after an administrator updates Power Platform data policies. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A. Successful creation permanently exempts the connector from data policies
B. Connector creation capability and governed use are separate; administrators can classify or block custom connectors and restrict which connector groups may be combined
C. Only Microsoft-built connectors can be governed by data policies
D. Recreating the connector with the same host automatically overrides the policy
questions.explanation: A maker's ability to define a connector doesn't grant an exception from tenant or environment governance. Power Platform data policies can classify custom connectors by host URL or connector identity and can prevent disallowed connector combinations or block use. Creation and policy permission are distinct gates.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Custom connector capability versus DLP governance

questions.question: A sponsor claims an invoice agent will deliver a 300% first-year ROI by multiplying estimated hours saved by labor cost. The estimate omits adoption, exception handling, evaluation, monitoring, model consumption, integration, and ongoing governance. What should the architect do before approving the business case?
options: A. Accept the estimate because labor savings are the only relevant AI benefit
B. Establish measured baselines, model realized adoption and benefits, include full-lifecycle TCO, and test conservative, expected, and optimistic scenarios
C. Exclude governance and monitoring because they are enterprise overhead rather than solution costs
D. Use the most optimistic model-consumption tier to protect the target ROI
questions.explanation: A defensible AI business case starts from measurable current-state baselines and distinguishes theoretical productivity from benefits actually realized through adoption. TCO must include implementation and recurring operating costs, including integration, model use, evaluation, monitoring, support, and governance. Scenario analysis exposes sensitivity instead of presenting one fragile point estimate.
questions.topic: D1.3 / ROI baselines, realized value, and lifecycle TCO

questions.question: A company needs common sales-email summaries and meeting preparation. A licensed Microsoft product already provides the required capability with acceptable controls, and the requirement contains no differentiating workflow. Which recommendation best follows a build-buy-extend decision sequence?
options: A. Buy or adopt the prebuilt capability first, and extend only for validated gaps
B. Build a custom agent runtime immediately to maximize code ownership
C. Train a custom language model before evaluating product functionality
D. Create multiple specialist agents because decomposition always improves ROI
questions.explanation: When a supported product already satisfies a commodity requirement and its governance needs, adopting it generally reduces delivery time, implementation risk, and lifecycle cost. Extension is justified by concrete unmet requirements; a custom build is justified when control or differentiation can't be achieved by buying or extending.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Build-buy-extend selection

questions.question: A business team needs an employee-support agent grounded in approved SharePoint content, using standard Power Platform connectors and workflows. Makers must maintain it through a graphical low-code experience, and no custom model runtime is required. Which platform is the best starting point?
options: A. Microsoft Copilot Studio
B. A fully custom Microsoft Foundry application with a bespoke orchestration engine
C. A custom-trained language model deployed directly to a GPU cluster
D. Azure Batch without an agent framework
questions.explanation: Copilot Studio is the direct fit for a graphical, low-code agent maintained by business makers and integrated with Microsoft knowledge and Power Platform workflows. Foundry is appropriate when developer control, custom code, models, or orchestration are material requirements; those needs aren't present here.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Platform selection for a low-code business agent

questions.question: A team needs to classify short internal service requests on edge hardware with strict latency and cost limits. Evaluation shows a catalog small language model meets the target accuracy without training. What should the architect recommend first?
options: A. Use the evaluated small model and monitor it against the acceptance criteria before considering customization
B. Train a new foundation model from scratch because every enterprise task requires proprietary weights
C. Select the largest available model regardless of latency and operating cost
D. Fine-tune immediately even though the baseline model already meets the requirement
questions.explanation: Model choice should be driven by evaluated task quality and nonfunctional constraints, not model size. If a smaller catalog model already meets accuracy, latency, deployment, and cost requirements, it is the simpler starting point. Customization adds data, evaluation, deployment, and maintenance obligations and should address a demonstrated gap.
questions.topic: D1.2 / SLM selection and custom-model justification

questions.question: Business units are independently launching agents with duplicated tools, inconsistent risk reviews, and no shared success metrics. Executives ask the AI Center of Excellence to take ownership of every implementation. Which operating model should the architect recommend?
options: A. A federated CoE that sets reusable standards, governance, enablement, intake, and measurement while domain teams retain accountable delivery ownership
B. A central CoE that writes and operates every agent indefinitely and removes business ownership
C. No central function; each team should define its own controls and metrics
D. A procurement-only committee that evaluates licenses but not risk, architecture, adoption, or value
questions.explanation: An AI CoE should create organizational capability: shared strategy, governance, reference patterns, reusable assets, enablement, prioritization, and value measurement. A federated model lets domain teams deliver with business context and accountability while the CoE reduces duplication and enforces consistent guardrails; making the CoE the permanent owner of every solution creates a bottleneck.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Federated AI Center of Excellence governance

questions.question: A manufacturer has a list of 40 proposed AI initiatives. Executives want to select a platform first and require every business unit to use it. Several proposals have no measurable outcome, unavailable grounding data, or an untested dependency on autonomous approvals. What should the architect do first?
options: A. Standardize on the platform with the largest model catalog, then rewrite every use case to fit it
B. Prioritize use cases by business outcome, feasibility, data readiness, risk, and expected value before selecting the appropriate solution pattern for each
C. Build all 40 initiatives as proofs of concept because feasibility cannot be assessed before deployment
D. Select the least expensive model for every initiative and use adoption as the only success measure
questions.explanation: Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework AI strategy guidance starts with the business use case and validates feasibility, value, data, cost, and risk before solution selection. A platform-first mandate can force unsuitable patterns and conceal initiatives that lack measurable outcomes or viable data. A prioritized portfolio gives each approved use case an explicit outcome and an architecture matched to its constraints.
questions.topic: D1.2 / AI adoption strategy and use-case prioritization
questions.source: AI-generated; grounded in current Microsoft Learn documentation

questions.question: Multiple teams copy successful prompts into production agents and edit them independently. After a policy change, the organization cannot determine which prompts are approved, what inputs they expect, or which evaluation set supports them. Which prompt-library guideline best addresses the problem?
options: A. Store only prompt text in a shared chat so makers can choose the newest-looking version
B. Maintain governed prompt assets with purpose, owner, input contract, version, approved examples, evaluation evidence, and change history
C. Prevent prompt reuse so every agent creates unique instructions directly in production
D. Treat temperature settings as sufficient version metadata because prompts are not solution components
questions.explanation: The AB-100 study guide explicitly requires guidelines for a prompt library and prompt engineering. A useful enterprise library is more than a text gallery: ownership, intended use, inputs, versions, examples, evaluation evidence, and change records make prompts discoverable, reusable, testable, and governable. Independent production copies create drift and make policy updates difficult to prove.
questions.topic: D1.2 / Governed prompt library
questions.source: AI-generated; grounded in current Microsoft Learn documentation

questions.question: An internal assistant receives a mix of simple rewriting requests and complex planning prompts. The team currently sends every request to its most capable model, producing unnecessary cost and latency. Quality must remain comparable for each request. What should the architect recommend?
options: A. Route requests round-robin so each model receives the same number regardless of prompt complexity
B. Deploy Microsoft Foundry model router and evaluate its quality, latency, and cost against representative traffic
C. Fine-tune the largest model to answer simple prompts more slowly but with identical billing
D. Let users choose a model by deployment name without any evaluation or default
questions.explanation: Microsoft Foundry model router is itself deployed as a model and routes prompts in real time to a suitable supported language model. It is intended to maintain comparable quality while improving cost, latency, and responsiveness. Representative evaluation is still required because routing benefits and acceptable quality depend on the workload; equal distribution and user guesswork do not account for prompt complexity.
questions.topic: D1.3 / Model router for cost-quality-latency balance
questions.source: AI-generated; grounded in current Microsoft Learn documentation

questions.question: A code-first business app needs two agent experiences: an interactive page generated for the current case, and a persistent stream where employees can review agent-proposed work and take action later. Which design maps the experiences correctly?
options: A. Use a generative page for the contextual interactive surface and an agent feed for the ongoing work stream
B. Use an agent feed to replace every app page and a generative page only for audit-log retention
C. Use a prompt library for the interactive surface and model router for the work stream
D. Use Computer Use for both experiences even though the application is being developed code-first
questions.explanation: The current AB-100 design objective and Microsoft Learn training distinguish code-first generative pages from agent feed applications. A generative page provides a contextual, agent-created interactive experience, while an agent feed presents persistent agent activity and proposed work that users can review and act on. Computer Use is for automating an existing interface when a suitable API or native integration is unavailable, not for defining these app experiences.
questions.topic: D2.1 / Code-first generative pages and agent feed
questions.source: AI-generated; grounded in current Microsoft Learn documentation

questions.question: A company is adapting a Copilot Studio text agent for a customer-service voice channel. The existing topics contain long paragraphs, dense option lists, and silent tool calls that can take 20 seconds. Which redesign is most appropriate?
options: A. Keep the text experience unchanged because speech synthesis automatically makes every interaction voice-appropriate
B. Design concise spoken turns, confirmations for consequential actions, interruption and fallback behavior, and progress handling for long-running operations; then test with real voice conversations
C. Remove confirmations because voice users cannot review consequential actions
D. Convert every topic to Computer Use so spoken responses no longer require orchestration
questions.explanation: Voice is an interaction behavior, not merely text read aloud. The architecture must account for short spoken turns, recognition errors, interruptions, silence, latency, fallback, and explicit confirmation before high-impact actions. Testing only the text transcript misses timing and conversational failures that occur in the voice channel.
questions.topic: D2.2 / Copilot Studio voice-mode behavior
questions.source: AI-generated; grounded in current Microsoft Learn documentation

questions.question: A sales organization uses a supported CRM, but a seller-facing agent also needs current discount eligibility from a secured pricing service. The service exposes a stable API, and eligibility must be checked at run time rather than copied into model knowledge. What should the architect design?
options: A. A governed connector or agent tool with a clear contract and delegated or workload authorization appropriate to the action
B. Fine-tune the language model on last quarter's discount table
C. Add discount values to the system prompt and grant all sellers administrator access
D. Use an ungrounded generative answer because CRM connectivity makes external authorization unnecessary
questions.explanation: Current transactional facts from a secured API belong behind a connector or tool, not in model weights or static instructions. The tool needs a precise description and input/output contract so orchestration can select it reliably, plus authorization that preserves the caller's permitted scope or a deliberately constrained workload identity. CRM connectivity does not automatically authorize a separate pricing system.
questions.topic: D2.1 / Sales agent connector and authorization design

questions.question: A service agent's overall resolution rate is unchanged, but complaints say handoffs from the mobile channel have become slower. The owner proposes rewriting the global instructions immediately. What should the architect recommend first?
